en: Salutations to Indirā, the consort of the Enemy of Madhu; she whose majesty is immeasurable, who bestows bliss upon practitioners, who grants the attainment of all prosperity, who destroys the darkness of misfortune, who is born from the ocean of nectar, and whose very form is of the nature of gold.

Having meditated with reverence upon the auspicious pair of feet of Śrī Brahmānvita-Śaṅkara, this beautiful commentary on the examination of the pulse (Nāḍīparīkṣā), entitled Vaidyapriyā, is now suddenly composed in the vernacular by Jyakṛṣṇadāsa for the pleasure of virtuous physicians. One should examine eight locations on the body of a person afflicted by disease.
The channels, urine, excrement, the tongue, sound, touch, sight, and form.

Like a lamp revealing objects to one who is ill, bewildered, and deluded, the channel of life (jīvanāḍī) reveals the nature of the arising of the humors (doṣas), whether they are individual, combined, or paired.
There is a certain channel located within the forearm that rests in the center;
it is called the "life-channel" (jīvanāḍī) by Nandin, the knower of reality.
Located specifically at the base of the thumb, it is examined with particular care;
for that channel, which pervades all the limbs, has been well-expounded by the former teachers.
Leaving aside one finger’s breadth below the base of the thumb, one should examine it with diligence; indeed, it is perceived through practice alone.
The vessel located at the base of the thumb is the witness of the life-force;
by its movement, pleasure and pain of the body are to be known by the wise.
One should diligently examine the pulse of women in the left hand and the left foot,
and specifically in the right side for men;
it is located below the ankle on the part of the big toe, or at the root of the big toe on the foot.
Leaving aside one finger's breadth at the wrist,
one should examine it by repeatedly pressing down from below with the hand using three fingers.
The most skilled physician, having gently grasped the patient’s elbow with his left hand,
should carefully examine the pulsation of the artery through the scriptures, his own experience, or the oral tradition.
In the beginning, the pulse flows as a carrier of wind (vāta); in the middle, it flows as a carrier of bile (pitta);
and at the end, through a disorder of phlegm (śleṣman), it is known as the threefold pulse.
When Vāta is predominant, the pulse is clearly perceptible on the surface of the index finger;
when Pitta is predominant, it is clear on the middle finger; and when Kapha is predominant, it is found on the third (ring) finger.
When wind and bile predominate, it is clearly manifest between the index finger and the middle finger;
when wind and phlegm predominate, it becomes distinct between the index finger and the ring finger.
It is clearly visible between the middle and ring fingers in cases of bile and phlegm;
it may also be distinctly manifest across all three fingers in cases of the triple-humoral disorder (sannipāta).
In the case of wind (vāta), the pulse has a crooked course; when carrying bile (pitta), it is flickering.

The *sthirā* type is said to be characterized by phlegm (*śleṣman*) and to exhibit all symptoms; it is pervasive and rendered stiff and numb by phlegm. One should recognize the mixed types by their combination of various symptoms.
In the case of a predominance of wind (vāta), the movement [of the vein] should be like that of a leech or a snake;
in the case of a predominance of bile (pitta), that vein has the movement of a crow or a frog;
and in the case of a predominance of phlegm (kapha), it has the movement of a swan or a pigeon.
In the case of the three doṣas, the pulse takes the gait of the partridge and the quail;
sometimes the pulse moves slowly, and sometimes it flows with great velocity.
That [condition] should be recognized by the best of physicians as a disease arising from the emergence of two doshas.
In diseases that cannot be cured by channel therapy, the movement [of the disease] flows slowly in some places, intensely in others, or is interrupted in some;
it is subtle in some places and gross in others.

If a vein is seen protruding above the skin and flows with extreme instability, it is declared to have the characteristics of being incurable; likewise, one that is slimy and excessively unstable is also incurable.
If it is attached above the thumb and flows evenly,
that [vein] should be known as faultless by those skilled in the characteristics of the *nāḍī*.
The pulse that flows with frequent pauses is a giver of death;
and a pulse that is excessively cold takes away the life of the patient.
The channel (nāḍī) becomes hot and forceful when fever breaks out,
as well as during agitation, anger, lust, and the arising of fear or anxiety.
The best of physicians should recognize that the channel whose movement has ceased is depleted;
for one whose bodily constituents are diminished and whose digestive fire is weak, it will certainly become even more sluggish.
A vein filled with blood becomes heavy and warm;
however, a vein filled with deficient blood becomes heavy and sluggish.
The pulse of one with a stimulated digestive fire is considered light and swift;
however, the pulse of one who is happy is steady and strong.
The pulse of one who is hungry is flickering, while it becomes steady when one is satiated;
likewise, in cases of pradara (menorrhagia), the pulse is steady and characterized by phlegm.
In the case of indigestion (ajīrṇa), however, the vein becomes hard and numb all around;
it is flickering when caused by undigested food (rasaja), and long as well as forceful in the case of bile (pitta).
In hunger, the pulse flows clear, rapid, and swift;
in fever, the pulse flows intensely and clearly due to the influence of pitta.
The pulse is said to be unctuous when it is flavorful and causes fainting during its flow;
the examination of the pulse in a healthy person is for the purpose of awakening knowledge of future diseases.
The channel that arises from the fear of falling under the weight [of existence], from fainting, and from cholera,
though it has become deeply constricted, once again attains life.
In cases of urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, and indigestion, the earth trembles swiftly.
One should observe the heavy pulse carrying wind (vāta) along with the fetus;
therein, the presence of bile (pitta) and wind should be declared by means of lightness and heaviness.
Furthermore, the wise should discern the division between the undigested (āma) and digested (pakva) states, as well as the days, months, and so forth.
That same vein, when carrying bile, is light; one should declare her to be one whose fetus has perished.
The earth does not experience trembling during affliction by disease, during crookedness [of posture], during a blow, during a startle, during physical exertion, or during loud, boisterous laughter.
A vein that is deep would be one that carries muscle tissue.
Long, thin, moving with the wind, uneven, and trembling;
the earth, which destroys life, is agitated by these signs of undigested accumulation.
For one afflicted by cold with moist limbs, lying down for a long time, the pulse— though subtle and slow—
gradually attains a throbbing movement endowed with strength.
When vāta is in its own place, it flows with a slightly curved course;
when kapha is in its own place, it is subtle in form, clear, and cold;
likewise, when pitta is in its own place, it is powerful, straight, and mobile.

The *nāḍī* is known to be crooked when there is an aggravation of wind (*vāta*), fierce when there is an aggravation of bile (*pitta*), and straight when there is an aggravation of phlegm (*śleṣman*);
thus it is described according to the individual humors.
When phlegm is diminished, the pulse flows with excessive movement of wind;
when wind is diminished and phlegm is excessive, it is slow; and when wind is diminished, phlegm is excessive, and bile is very slight, it becomes distinct only after a long time.
The pulse born of natural vāta is gentle, subtle, steady, and slow;
that born of vāta and pitta is slightly tremulous, crooked, and hard.
A pulse born from phlegm and wind (kapha-vāta) is thick, flickering, cold, and slow;
a pulse arising from bile and phlegm (pitta-kapha) is subtle, cold, and steady.
When there is an excess of pitta, she becomes fickle due to the consumption of pungent and similar substances; she constantly eats food that is harsh and dry, which increases vāta.
The pulse of one with a predominance of Vāta will be rough and resemble a small lump;
the pulse born from the disorder of Śleṣman (Kapha) is slow, cold, and resembles a thread.
Of one desiring to sport, who has abandoned delight and is moving like the wind.
It is like the bile of a child whose urge is suppressed or who has been pierced by a thorn;
it is also like the phlegm of one who is sleepy, lethargic, satiated, or arrogant.
Equal, subtle, and characterized by minute pulsations, it is proclaimed to occur when the waste matter is undigested;
irregular, hard, and gross, it is proclaimed to result from the residue of waste matter.
Due to blood loss, indigestion, emesis, purgation, depletion of vitality,
the binding of hemorrhaging, fainting and similar conditions, or from the dullness of the digestive fire, the channel of a living being flows like a trembling thread.
A pulse that is devoid of strength, subtle, and known to be filled with phlegm (kapha),
which is like a thread, slow, and cold, is born from the disorder of cold (śīta-doṣa).
When combined with phlegm and bile, it moves very slowly in one who eats sparingly;
however, when combined with blood, it especially causes excessive burning and floods the body.
If the channel flows in the middle of the hand and is both long and rapid,
then indeed the impurities of that person are filled with blood.
In a fever caused by Vāta, the breath is crooked, unsteady, and cold to the touch;
in a fever caused by Pitta, it is rapid, straight, long, and swift.
In cases of kapha, the pulse is slow, very steady, cold, and slimy;
in a fever caused by pitta, the vein flows thin like a lotus fiber, straight, and long.
It quickly brings about severe indigestion due to the presence of impurities;
it is described as being thick and hard, and it throbs rapidly when the vital wind (māruta) is intense.
Formerly mild, the pulse gradually becomes fierce;
it quickly attains a state of fever, coldness, or trembling.
This [vein] is considered the mother of diseases such as those occurring every day;
it is visible in the *sirā* when possessed by spirits (*bhūtagraha*) and in the fever that will occur every day.
Sometimes moving slowly and sometimes flowing with great speed, she should be known as arising from the provocation of two humors; and when displaced from her proper site, she destroys.
In blood-bile (raktapitta), the pulse flows slowly, is hard, and straight;
in phlegm-cough (śleṣmakāsa), it is steady and slow; and in asthma (śvāsa), it becomes rapid in its movement.
In the case of the king of diseases (consumption), the pulse is proclaimed to be like the movement of a serpent;
in cases of alcoholism, it becomes subtle, hard, and numb all around.
In the disease of hemorrhoids, the pulse is firm, slow, sometimes crooked, and sometimes straight;
in diarrhea, however, it is slow, like that of a leech in the cold season.
When there is an increase in flesh, that pulse indicates the onset of fever and diarrhea;
a vein resembling a dead snake portends the disease of *grahaṇī*.
In urinary obstruction, it becomes swollen with frequent discharge and throbbing;
in urinary disorders (prameha), the vein is dull, subtle, and repeatedly distended.
In jaundice (pāṇḍuroga), the pulse is unstable, intense, and moves in a manner visible and invisible;
in leprosy (kuṣṭha), however, the vessel is hard, steady, and lacks movement.
In a disease of wind (vāta), it is firm; when obstructed by all [humors], it possesses all symptoms;
in phlegm (balāsa), it is accompanied by throbbing, subtle, and fast-moving.
In disorders above the clavicle, having understood their characteristics according to the strength of the respective doshas, the physician should prescribe the downward movement [of the doshas].
That which is hard like the sun or moon and hot is the disease located in the blood.
The channel that sustains the *sannipāta* [disorder] is manifest in its movement by both cold and heat; it is extremely subtle and possesses great velocity, yet it subsides during a *sannipāta*.
However, when it becomes cold and possesses a moist velocity, it is the slayer of that patient.
That which moves after having repeatedly come to rest is known as "life-destroying";
being both extremely sharp and cold, it undoubtedly kills one's life.
If the pulse is rapid at the end of delirium, the fever will be equal to fire at midday;
his life lasts for one day, and on the second day, death is certain.
At the time of death, the channel becomes worn out like a hand-drum;
it is thin at the top and curves downward at the bottom.
One should designate as incurable that vein which is very high, unstable, which carries flesh,
which is extremely thin, and which is crooked.
If a person's pulse at the mouth is steady and appears like the flash of lightning, his life lasts for one day; on the second day, death is certain.
Flowing very slowly, or crookedly, or agitated, or even remaining still for long intervals, the subtle pulse perishes;
it falters from its usual position and again touches the finger—through such various symptoms arising from a combination of humors (sannipāta), it is incurable.

The sages who know the movement of the channels declare that channel to be incurable, which first carries the course of bile and then the course of wind, sustaining phlegm while repeatedly causing it to wander from its own place as if mounted upon a wheel; which possesses intensity, moves with the gait of a peacock, extends subtlety, and is difficult to master.
Just as a woodcutter chops wood with great force,
moving again and again after pausing, so too does that which arises from the combination [of the humors] occur.
If it trembles and throbbs like a thread and then touches the finger, one should know that this channel is tamasic and incurable; one should avoid it from afar.
If a sharp pulse flows in the mouth, or sometimes flows cold,
and a slimy sweat arises, one does not live beyond seven nights.
If there is coldness in the body, breathlessness in the mouth, and the pulse is intensely burning, his life remains for only half a month; so it has been declared by those who understand the pulse.
When there is no pulse at the mouth [of the nostrils], coldness in the center, and exhaustion on the outside,
and the pulse flows as faintly as a single thread, he does not live for three nights.
If the pulse that arose with force on the previous day becomes cold and its momentum is obstructed on the following day, then there is danger from a sannipāta (combined derangement of the humors).
If the fever becomes excessively like fire on the preceding day,
and when the pulse flows continuously for only a single lava,
then death occurs on the fourth day at the location of the patient's mouth.
When nothing at all is seen as the mouth suddenly cracks open,
then one should know that for the sick, death is certain on the second day.
When the channel, its force destroyed, does not throb at all,
then the death of the patient shall occur in the middle of the day.
If the moving channel, resembling a hand-drum (ḍamaruka), should wander continuously in the region of the mouth,
death will occur for the afflicted person within one day.
If it becomes exceedingly subtle, distinct, rapid, forceful, full, or moist,
and dies again and again, then one should know it to be incurable.
In the case of a healthy person, the pulse located at the base of the thumb should appear first, because there is no manifestation [of disease].
If it becomes subtle through further proliferation, the man dies in three days;
if it rises with the speed of lightning above the hands, the man dies in seven days.

When the network of channels has become tranquil and the activity of the senses has come to rest; when a subtle transformation of a non-warm nature has occurred, resulting in a state of total coldness;

when the path of the mind-self is empty, devoid of vibration, and the movement of perception has perished; when the sun is established in the nature of the moon and the multitude of qualities has been realized—then this fivefold state is to be proclaimed.
The system of channels and so forth undergoes transformation, reaches supreme peace, and attains subtlety; or else, its luster undergoes reversal once it has abandoned the vital wind of its own path.
Indeed, when ignorance has reached emptiness and the faculty of cognition is stilled, the sun and moon likewise clearly come to their end when they are obstructed.

With dry lips, even when the mouth is darkened, with teeth and nails turning pale, the region of the nose cold, the eyes bloodshot and one eye rolling, with hands and feet trembling, and suffering from the falling out of the ears;
with breath that is either cold or hot, gasping for air, the body cold and shaking, agitated and devoid of all mental activity—the human being thus manifests at the time of death in every respect.
Having overcome the five [hindrances] five times over, they cultivate the five faculties within the five [objects].
Having cultivated the five faculties within the five, they return to the state of the five at the time of destruction.
In a person whose vital energy is whirled about by wind, the pulse throbs excessively and irregularly; it does not exhibit the arrival of bile and becomes sluggish during the onset of slowness.

It attains abundance through the influence of its dependence on the rasa-constituent, yet when depleted and abandoned by rasa, it leads one to labored breathing and finally reaches stillness with unmoving breaths at the time of men's end.
When the earth vibrates thirty times by the measure of a single breath even while one is in a healthy state, then the sick person certainly lives; it is not otherwise.
If the body is cool while the pulse is certainly very hot,
the best of physicians should know that fever has entered within him.
Knowing the earth to be facing death, one should not treat a patient afflicted by disease;
instead, one should administer the medicine of Rāma’s name for the sake of the next world.
